endorsements.title: Principles for augmented intelligence development, deployment, and use
endorsements.quote: Health care AI requires a risk-based approach where the level of scrutiny, validation, and oversight should be proportionate to the overall potential of disparate harm and consequences the AI system might introduce.

endorsements.title: Toward a responsible future: recommendations for AI-enabled clinical decision support
endorsements.issuer: Journal of the American Medical Informatics Association : JAMIA
endorsements.quote: Such systems should be designed to provide user-friendly summaries for both clinicians and patients and support documentation encompassing: The goal and specific questions asked of the AI.

endorsements.title: Ethical Considerations for Generative Artificial Intelligence in Plastic Surgery
endorsements.issuer: Plastic and reconstructive surgery. Global open
endorsements.quote: Surgeons should disclose the use of genAI for surgical decision-making or any other purpose to their patients and in medical notes as they would for any other clinical intervention.

endorsements.title: Patient Perspectives on Artificial Intelligence in Medical Imaging
endorsements.quote: When AI plays a significant role in shaping diagnostic or treatment recommendations, clinicians could consider including information in imaging reports or after-visit summaries about: The specific role AI played in the diagnostic process (eg, prioritizing findings, generating a differential diagnosis, or suggesting treatment pathways).

endorsements.title: Artificial Intelligence-Assisted Clinical Decision-Making: A Perspective on Advancing Personalized Precision Medicine for Elderly Diabetes Patients
endorsements.quote: Additionally, establishing comprehensive decision-tracking systems is crucial to document AI-assisted decisions, ensuring accountability and traceability.

endorsements.title: Artificial Intelligence (AI) and Emergency Medicine: Balancing Opportunities and Challenges
endorsements.quote: Additionally, requiring critical decisions prompted by AI to be documented with explanations can increase trust.

endorsements.title: The Ethical Boundaries of Chairside Generative Artificial Intelligence in Dental Education
endorsements.quote: GenAI use must be documented in patient records.

endorsements.title: Navigating the artificial intelligence landscape in trauma, critical care and emergency general surgery: insights from the American Association for the Surgery of Trauma (AAST) 2025 Annual Meeting Panel Discussion
endorsements.quote: Institutional policies that define appropriate indications for AI use, override protocols, documentation of when and how AI was consulted, and thresholds for pausing or updating models were highlighted as core elements of responsible implementation.

endorsements.title: Clinical Artificial Intelligence (AI) Liability in the MENA Region: a Comparative Analysis of Hospital, Physician, Suppliers, and Vendor Responsibility
endorsements.quote: clinicians should transparently document when and how AI was used, record the rationale for accepting or overriding outputs, and disclose material AI involvement to patients as part of informed consent when it could influence clinical choices

endorsements.title: NAIL-G: a conceptual best-fit framework for nursing ai literacy and governance anchored in socio-technical safety science
endorsements.quote: Documenting AI involvement in clinical and educational artefacts, where appropriate.

endorsements.title: Educational Frameworks for Diagnostic Decision-Making in AI-Enhanced Head and Neck Pathology
endorsements.quote: Learners and clinicians should be able to articulate how AI tools have influenced their reasoning, justify their reliance on specific outputs, and clearly communicate uncertainty to colleagues and patients.

endorsements.title: Personal Health Large Language Models and the Negotiation of Medical Authority in Clinical Care: Opportunities, Risks, and Governance
endorsements.quote: For moderate-risk or high-risk advice, including safety-critical items, minimum documentation should capture the clinically relevant AI-generated claim or recommendation, the reason for accepting, modifying, or rejecting it, any patient preference that materially affected the decision, and the final shared plan.

endorsements.title: Ethical considerations for multimodal artificial intelligence in healthcare
endorsements.quote: For AI-generated or AI-assisted clinical text, metadata should preserve source inputs, model version, human reviewer, substantive edits, verification status, and final sign-off.

endorsements.title: A Human-Governed Clinical Informatics Framework for Safe AI-Assisted Mental Health Counseling: Secondary Framework Development and Requirement Mapping Study
endorsements.quote: At minimum, AI disclosure should be required when AI output influences the clinical record, triage workflow, or client-facing communication.

endorsements.title: NeonatAIlogy: The GIRISH (Goal, Input, Role, Iterative Refinement, Safety Verification, and Human Accountability) Framework for Structured, Human-Accountable Artificial Intelligence in Neonatal Intensive Care
endorsements.quote: Document that a named clinician made the decision.

commentary.bottom_line: Fifteen sources endorse documenting AI influence on care in the medical record, but no supplied study tests whether this practice improves traceability, accountability, or patient outcomes, or what burden it adds. The recommendation rests on expert opinion and professional guidance alone.

perspectives.view: The supplied endorsements are one guidance document and commentaries. No study tests the practice, and no study documents the hazard. Under GRADE conventions, expert opinion does not yield a certainty rating for effect, so the certainty is best described as no direct evidence. Agreement among sources shows consensus, not effectiveness.

The recommendation asks for documentation that minimizes administrative burden, yet no supplied study measures the time cost, documentation fidelity, or clinician uptake of any recording approach. Endorsers propose content ranging from a simple note of AI use to the question asked, the output, and the reason for accepting or overriding it. Those options may differ in burden, and none has been compared.

No supplied study shows that untraceable AI influence has caused missed errors or blocked incident review. No study shows that documentation helps reviewers find AI-related failures. The expected benefit, which is reconstructing decisions after harm, remains a plausible mechanism that has not been tested.

commentary.research_gap: Studies are needed that compare documentation approaches, such as structured EHR fields, automated logging, and free-text notes, on clinician time, completeness, and usefulness in later case review or incident investigation. Studies are also needed to measure how often undocumented AI influence impairs accountability.
commentary.underserved_note: No study tested this practice, so no evidence covers Medicaid, safety-net, limited English proficiency, or low-literacy populations. Whether documentation or related patient disclosure works for these groups, including through after-visit summaries in plain language or in languages other than English, is unknown.
